person.name: Albert_Einstein
person.summary: Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist who developed the theories of special and general relativity and made seminal contributions to quantum theory and statistical physics. His 1905 annus mirabilis papers transformed modern physics, and his mass–energy equivalence relation E = mc² became iconic. Awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his explanation of the photoelectric effect, he held academic posts in Zurich, Prague, Berlin, and Princeton. A Jewish refugee from Nazi Germany, he became a prominent public intellectual, speaking on pacifism, Zionism, civil liberties, and the dangers of nuclear weapons.

chapters.headline: Childhood and Formative Schooling
chapters.description: From his birth in Ulm through his secondary schooling in Munich and Aarau, Einstein’s early years combined family upheaval with an intense, largely self-directed immersion in mathematics and science.

chapters.headline: Polytechnic Years and Annus Mirabilis
chapters.description: Einstein’s studies in Zurich, early struggles for academic employment, work as a Swiss patent clerk, and his revolutionary 1905 research that reshaped modern physics.

chapters.headline: Relativity and International Fame
chapters.description: From his move to Zurich and Prague through his Berlin professorship, general relativity, and the 1919 eclipse confirmation, Einstein became the world’s most celebrated physicist.

chapters.headline: From Berlin Luminary to Exile
chapters.description: Already a global icon, Einstein deepened his engagement with quantum theory and politics, then broke with Nazi Germany in 1933 and began a new life in the United States.

chapters.headline: Princeton, Nuclear Age, Final Years
chapters.description: As an American citizen and Institute for Advanced Study professor, Einstein reflected on quantum theory, warned of nuclear dangers, pursued a unified field theory, and lived out his final years in Princeton.

events.title: Birth in Ulm
events.description: Albert Einstein was born on 14 March 1879 in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire, to Hermann Einstein, a salesman and engineer, and Pauline Koch. The family were secular Ashkenazi Jews. Within a year they moved to Munich, where his father and uncle founded an electrical engineering firm, giving the young Albert early exposure to technical discussions and apparatus.

events.title: Graduation in Aarau
events.description: After leaving the rigid Luitpold Gymnasium in Munich, Einstein completed his secondary education at the Argovian cantonal school in Aarau, Switzerland. In September 1896 he passed his Matura examinations with strong grades in history, physics, algebra, and geometry. This Swiss school’s liberal, discussion-based teaching style contrasted sharply with his earlier experience and left a lasting mark on his intellectual outlook.

images.caption: Albert Einstein’s 1896 certificate of maturity from the Argovian cantonal school in Aarau, showing his final examination grades.

events.title: Studies at Zurich Polytechnic
events.description: In 1897, at age seventeen, Einstein enrolled in the mathematics and physics teaching diploma program at the Swiss Federal Polytechnic School in Zurich (later ETH Zürich). Over four years he studied advanced mathematics, theoretical and experimental physics, and mechanics, befriending fellow student Marcel Grossmann and forming an intense scientific and personal partnership with Mileva Marić. He graduated in 1900, qualified to teach mathematics and physics.

images.caption: Albert Einstein with colleagues at the physics laboratory of the Swiss Federal Polytechnic School in Zurich.

events.title: Patent Office Appointment in Bern
events.description: After several unsuccessful attempts to obtain an academic post following graduation, Einstein secured a permanent position in 1902 as a technical expert, third class, at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern. Evaluating patent applications for electromagnetic devices provided him with a steady income and regular hours, while the relative intellectual isolation encouraged him to pursue independent theoretical work in his spare time, laying the groundwork for his 1905 breakthroughs.

images.caption: Albert Einstein at his desk in the Swiss Patent Office in Bern, where he worked while developing his early revolutionary papers.

events.title: Marriage to Mileva Marić
events.description: In January 1903, Einstein married Mileva Marić, a Serbian physicist and mathematician whom he had met as a fellow student at the Zurich Polytechnic. They settled in Bern, where Einstein worked at the patent office and Mileva set aside her own scientific ambitions as they started a family. Their complex personal and intellectual relationship has since been the subject of considerable historical debate.

images.caption: Albert Einstein with his first wife, Mileva Marić, photographed during their years together in Switzerland.

events.title: Annus Mirabilis Papers
events.description: While employed full‑time at the Bern patent office, Einstein in 1905 published four epoch‑making papers in Annalen der Physik. They provided a light‑quantum explanation of the photoelectric effect, a theory of Brownian motion, the special theory of relativity, and the mass–energy equivalence relation E = mc². Together, these works transformed the foundations of modern physics and later earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.

images.caption: Cover page of Albert Einstein’s 1905 doctoral dissertation submitted to the University of Zurich, from the same year as his annus mirabilis papers.

events.title: First Professorship in Zurich
events.description: In 1909, after obtaining his PhD from the University of Zurich in 1905, Einstein left the Bern patent office to accept his first full professorship in theoretical physics at the University of Zurich. This marked his transition from civil servant to professional academic physicist and gave him more time and institutional support to deepen his work on radiation, statistical mechanics, and the emerging quantum theory.

events.title: Completion of General Relativity
events.description: Working in Berlin during World War I, Einstein in 1915 presented the final form of his general theory of relativity to the Prussian Academy of Sciences. Extending his 1905 special relativity and drawing on advanced tensor calculus, the new theory described gravitation as the curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy. General relativity radically revised Newtonian mechanics on cosmic scales and provided a new framework for understanding cosmology and gravitating systems.

images.caption: Albert Einstein in his office at the University of Berlin, photographed in 1920 during the period when general relativity was being intensely studied and debated.

events.title: Divorce from Mileva Marić
events.description: On 14 February 1919, a court in Zurich granted Einstein and Mileva Marić a divorce after five years of separation. Under the settlement, Einstein agreed that if he were to receive a Nobel Prize, the prize money would go to Marić. Their marriage had increasingly strained under his growing scientific preoccupations, personal differences, and his relationship with his cousin Elsa Löwenthal, whom he married later that year.

events.title: Eclipse Confirmation of Relativity
events.description: On 29 May 1919, British expeditions led by Arthur Eddington to Sobral, Brazil, and Príncipe, off West Africa, photographed a total solar eclipse to test Einstein’s prediction that starlight would be deflected by the Sun’s gravity. Their analysis showed a deflection consistent with general relativity and significantly larger than the Newtonian expectation. When the results were announced later that year, Einstein became an international scientific celebrity, and his theory of gravitation widely accepted.

images.caption: One of the 1919 solar eclipse plates from Sobral used to measure the deflection of starlight by the Sun, confirming Einstein’s prediction.

events.title: Nobel Prize in Physics
events.description: In 1921, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded Einstein the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1921, citing “his services to theoretical physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.” The prize, formally presented in 1922, recognised his decisive role in establishing the quantum nature of light, rather than his then‑controversial relativity theories. In accordance with his divorce agreement, the Nobel money went to his first wife, Mileva Marić.

images.caption: Official 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics portrait of Albert Einstein.

events.title: Escape from Nazi Germany
events.description: While Einstein was visiting the United States in early 1933, Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany and began purging Jews from academic and public life. Einstein, horrified by Nazi antisemitism, decided not to return. On 26 May 1933 he travelled from Ostend to Dover, as recorded on his British landing card, and then on to Oxford. Soon afterward he resigned from the Prussian Academy of Sciences and gave up his German citizenship, becoming a prominent symbol of the exodus of Jewish and anti‑Nazi intellectuals.

images.caption: Einstein’s British landing card from 26 May 1933, documenting his arrival at Dover after leaving Nazi Germany.

events.title: Einstein–Szilard Letter to Roosevelt
events.description: On 2 August 1939, physicist Leo Szilard drafted a letter, signed by Albert Einstein, to U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt warning that recent discoveries in nuclear fission could enable Nazi Germany to build extremely powerful bombs. The letter urged the United States to begin its own research and stockpile uranium. Delivered to Roosevelt in October, it prompted the creation of U.S. uranium committees and helped set in motion what became the Manhattan Project, though Einstein himself did not work on the project.

images.caption: Scan of the August 2, 1939 letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, drafted by Leo Szilard and signed by Albert Einstein, urging U.S. action on nuclear fission research.

events.title: Becomes an American Citizen
events.description: In 1940, having settled at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, Einstein was granted United States citizenship while retaining his Swiss nationality. As a German‑Jewish refugee from Nazism, he used his new position to speak out on behalf of fellow refugees, civil liberties, and, later, against the unrestrained use of nuclear weapons. He remained in Princeton for the rest of his life.

images.caption: Albert Einstein receiving his certificate of American citizenship from Judge Phillip Forman in 1940.

events.title: Death in Princeton
events.description: Albert Einstein died on 18 April 1955 at Princeton Hospital in New Jersey after suffering a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. By then he was globally revered not only as the architect of relativity but also as a moral voice who had spoken on pacifism, Zionism, civil rights, and the perils of nuclear war. He left unfinished his decades‑long quest for a unified field theory and remains one of the most influential scientists in history.
